content: When data is entered and verified, the DHIS 2 system facilitates the automatic generation of routine reports, which can be predefined for efficiency. Additionally, DHIS 2 supports the creation of analytical reports by comparing indicators across facilities or over time. Outputs such as graphs, maps, reports, and health profiles can be generated, and these should be routinely analyzed and acted upon by managers. DHIS 2 is an open-source, globally distributed system managed by the Health Information Systems Programme (HISP), with developers in India, Ireland, Norway, Tanzania, and Vietnam. The University of Oslo, with support from NORAD Development, coordinates its development. Sentinel monitoring facilities are strategically selected sites that collect extensive datasets to address complex clinical questions, such as drug resistance surveillance. These facilities use electronic platforms for data collection and require close monitoring for accuracy and completeness. By focusing on sentinel sites, the burden of data collection on other routine reporting facilities is reduced. Variables that do not vary by location or service quality can be collected at a few facilities and extrapolated to the larger population. Sentinel sites often require additional staff, including research officers skilled in data manipulation, to address ad-hoc questions from provincial or national authorities. These sites are sometimes chosen due to additional resources provided by academic or non-governmental partners. Good data management practices involve planning strategies for data storage, management, and usage during the design phase of strategic information and monitoring and evaluation (M&E) plans. Effective data management includes consistent data collection, secure storage, data cleaning, regular backups, and the ability to transfer data between software systems for analysis. Even with standardized procedures, data must be checked for inaccuracies or missing information through a process called data cleaning. Presenting data appropriately is also critical, as it transforms raw data into actionable information, enabling clear findings and substantiated recommendations. Data accessibility is important for verification and further use, such as systematic reviews or meta-analyses. Key elements of good data management include data security, confidentiality, access, sharing, use of unique identifiers, and interoperability. Unique identifiers (UIs) are alphanumeric codes assigned to individuals within a data management system. They enhance linkage across healthcare services, improving care efficiency and effectiveness. UIs allow ministries of health to reliably link all health data for an individual, enabling accurate counts of those eligible for care, tracking service delivery progress, and evaluating impact. UIs also provide healthcare providers with a comprehensive longitudinal history of a patient’s medical care, informing better clinical decisions. UIs are routinely used for patient care coordination, clinical documentation, administrative functions, and aggregating patient data for research and statistical reporting. In regions with networked systems, implementing UIs is straightforward with the right software. However, decentralized systems face challenges in generating UIs. Mobile phones offer an opportunity to implement a nationwide patient management index that generates UIs. Central servers can store patient registration data and generate UIs for unregistered patients. Reception staff can use mobile phones to access the central server, look up patients, or register new ones. Protecting the confidentiality and security of individual health information is critical, especially when using UIs. An advantage of UIs is their enhanced confidentiality, as they do not use names or other personally identifiable information. However, challenges include difficulty in tracking patients outside the healthcare system and the risk of duplicate registrations. Mechanisms must be in place to monitor UI usage and address breaches. Interoperability is essential for health information systems, enabling seamless data exchange and interpretation between systems. Consolidating data into a single national database allows for in-depth analysis of access, services, epidemiological trends, and population health profiles. Structured data exchange templates using health data and IT standards should be adopted. Ministries of health should establish working groups to oversee interoperability and data standards. Achieving interoperability is complex but critical for clinical and public health systems. It requires ongoing updates to software as protocols and policies evolve. Data security and encryption are essential to protect patient confidentiality. Health management information systems (HMIS) are designed to assist in managing and planning health programs by collecting predefined data from multiple services and feeding it into a national database. HMIS software may collect aggregated clinical, immunological, and outcome data, which should be accessible to program managers at all levels. Data quality must remain high to inform policy effectively. All software used in healthcare facilities should be interoperable with the national HMIS software. Over time, countries should aim to eliminate parallel reporting systems. High-quality data is critical for monitoring program effectiveness and ensuring high-quality care. The Data Quality Review (DQR) framework, developed by WHO, the Global Fund, and Gavi, assesses data quality across dimensions such as completeness, timeliness, internal consistency, and external consistency. It identifies whether data issues are program-specific or systemic, providing valuable insights into the reliability of health facility data.
